sm: The hosts, Myrna Brown and Mary Reichard, open the Thanksgiving Day episode with the news. Officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade to Saturday because of forecast wind gusts of fifty to sixty miles per hour, so NBC will rerun last year's parade. President Trump hosted NATO chief Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago with the war in Ukraine on the agenda, and the Army destroyed the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide, nearly five tons, in a controlled detonation in Iowa. The economy grew at a 4.3 percent annual pace over the summer, revised up from 3.4 percent, while inflation over the past year rose to 3.8 percent. Officials also described planned tariff increases, including a 20 percent tariff on Chinese goods.

Washington State's Initiative 638 takes effect soon and requires athletes in girls' sports to get a doctor's note verifying they are female. The ACLU sued on November 9 for transgender athletes and for female students who object to the verification, and Female Athletes United wants to join in support of the law. Medical groups warn it could require costly genetic testing or invasive exams, though the law lets doctors choose among reproductive anatomy, genetics or testosterone levels. A hearing on an injunction is set for next Thursday. Then Dr. Michael Artigues of the American College of Pediatricians explains a request to the residency accrediting council to protect the conscience rights of pediatric residents who object to so-called sex-rejecting procedures.

Dr. Artigues says residents who object could be exposed to guidelines from groups like WPATH, and that finishing residency in good standing matters for board eligibility and insurance. He says the letter with Do No Harm is mostly meant to head off future problems, modeled on protections for OB-GYN residents. On Colorado's Proposition 135, he says it bans only surgeries, while hormones and puberty blockers remain, and he is not sure Colorado will enforce it. He is encouraged that more than half of states have passed similar laws. A report then begins on hackers who attacked grocery refrigeration systems in Europe, with shoppers and a refrigeration industry veteran explaining why stores monitor cold storage remotely.

The refrigeration story continues. Hackers in France and elsewhere in Europe triggered defrost cycles in hundreds of stores, driving some refrigerators to 120 degrees and costing tens of millions of dollars. A cybersecurity expert at Forescout blames default passwords and older systems that can no longer be patched. He thinks the attack may make American systems safer as companies reduce internet exposure, and he says responsibility must be clearly assigned among stores, vendors and contractors. A light segment recounts the White House turkey pardon, where Feathers hid in the bushes. Then Cynthia Scott, author of a book for America's 250th birthday, says the Pilgrims and Puritans built their lives, schools and the Mayflower Compact on a biblical worldview.

Cynthia Scott describes the founders' worldview as biblical and broad, meaning true to the Bible and applied to every part of life. Asked how to honor God at a divided Thanksgiving table, she suggests starting by giving thanks and praising God for what he has done in America. Next, commentator Cal Thomas tells how Sarah Josepha Hale, a magazine editor and author of Mary Had a Little Lamb, campaigned for a national Thanksgiving. Lincoln proclaimed it in 1863, after earlier presidents had issued one-time proclamations. Thomas quotes Lincoln crediting God for the nation's blessings and blaming the Civil War on forgetting him. The hosts preview tomorrow's Culture Friday and a review of the movie Hexed.
